newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - MCI sees PCS rates "competitive".
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - MCI sees PCS rates "competitive".

text.p: MCI Communications Corp's wide-ranging pact to buy wireless communications air-time from NextWave Telecom Inc was done at "very competitive rates" or MCI would not have agreed to the deal, an MCI official said.
Under terms of the deal, MCI said it will buy at least 10 billion minutes of Personal Communications Services (PCS) capacity from NextWave over the next 10 years.

In a telephone interview, Whitey Bluestein, MCI's vice president of MCI's wireless strategy and development, said that, "They are very competitive rates or we wouldn't have entered into a 10-year deal."
Bluestein sought to distinguish the pact from a simple reseller agreement in which MCI buys wireless network capacity from NextWave and resells it to its own customers.
He underlined that a key motivation behind the deal was that MCI and NextWave had agreed to interconnect their networks to offer a combined set of communications services.
"Interconnection is what distinguishes this from resale," Bluestein said. "We'll be plugging our networks in together."
He said the wireless deal bolsters MCI's ability to compete in local phone markets by allowing it to bypass the incumbent Regional Bells to connect directly to customers.
"(This technology) becomes one more weapon in our arsenal," Bluestein said. "This is one more way to go the last mile without using the local telephone company."
By "last mile" he was referring to customers concentrated in the geographical area typically covered by a local phone company's central switching offices.

So-called "wireless local loop technology" would allow MCI to connect its land-line network to customers via NextWave's network without paying access charges to the local regional Bell company in any given city.
The NextWave deal provides MCI with the capacity to offer PCS services to more than 110 million customers in 63 U.S. cities, including 29 of the top 50 markets.

Earlier Monday, in a joint conference call held by officials of the two companies, NextWave said it plans to begin operating its wireless network by mid-1997 and that most of the 63 markets would be up and running by the end of 1998.

Bluestein said that as soon as NextWave's networks are in operation, "We will be there," although he qualified the statement by noting that the network would have to meet MCI's standards for voice quality first.

The MCI official said the deal with NextWave was not exclusive and that long-distance carrier expected to sign additional resale agreements in the future allowing it over time to offer wireless service throughout the country.
"I am very relaxed about our ability to fill out our footprint going forward," Bluestein said of MCI's U.S. plans.
His comment highlighted the flexibility of MCI's conservative stance on wireless infrastructure investments.

Rival national wireless networks now being created by AT&T Corp, Sprint Spectrum, the Sprint /cable industry venture, and PCS PrimeCo, the Regional Bell-backed venture have invested heavily to buy government wireless licences.
In addition, these competitiors must invest heavily in the capital infrastructure necessary to operate PCS networks, the next generation digital cellular communications network.
By contrast, MCI has stayed on the sidelines, opting instead to remain a reseller of wireless services on network built and financed by other players.
"Our strategy is not to invest in (PCS wireless radio) spectrum," Bluestein said. "We will let other people do that."
"Our strength is in marketing, merchandising and integration."
-- Eric Auchard, New York Newsdesk, 212-859-1736
